d: A biopsy confirms most cancers. How it is done, what the pathologist looks at and how to read the main parts of a report.
n: Why a biopsy is needed A mammogram, a scan or a blood test can raise the suspicion of cancer, but cells almost always need to be seen under the microscope to confirm it. A biopsy means taking a tissue sample, and pathology is the medical specialty that examines it. The pathologist's report answers three questions: is it cancer? What exact type? What features will help choose treatment? There are a few exceptions where diagnosis can be made without a biopsy, such as some liver cancers with a typical pattern on imaging. n: What they are for Imaging helps to detect a lesion, guide a biopsy , find out how far the cancer has spread ( stage ), plan surgery or radiotherapy , assess response to treatment and carry out follow-up . Each test answers some questions better than others, so the choice depends on the tumour and the clinical question. d: Two words found in almost every report, and often confused. Stage tells you how far the cancer has spread; grade, what its cells look like.
n: Two different ideas Stage describes how far the cancer has spread in the body: the size of the tumour, whether it affects lymph nodes and whether it has reached other organs. Grade describes how the cells look under the microscope: the more different they are from normal cells, the higher the grade and, generally, the faster they grow. A tumour can be small and localised (low stage) but high grade, or the other way round. Both help decide treatment. The TNM system The most widely used staging system for solid tumours, produced by the AJCC and the UICC: T (tumour): size and local extent, from T

d: What biomarkers are, how a tumour's genetic changes are studied and why finding a target does not guarantee an effective treatment.
n: What a biomarker is A biomarker is a measurable feature that tells us something about the tumour. In oncology they are used to: Classify the tumour precisely (for example, subtypes of breast cancer or glioma). Estimate the outlook . Predict whether a treatment will work: the most useful in practice. d: Between 5 and 10% of cancers are due to an inherited predisposition. When to suspect it, what genetic counselling is and what can be done with the result.
n: How many cancers are inherited All cancers are caused by changes in the genes of cells, but the vast majority are acquired during life. Only 5 to 10% are due to an inherited variant that greatly increases risk. Cancer is also common, so several cases in a family do not always mean an inherited cause. d: Surgery is still the treatment that cures the most solid cancers. What it is for, what margins and sentinel nodes are, and how it has moved towards less aggressive techniques.
n: What it is for Surgery is the oldest cancer treatment and still the one that cures the most localised solid tumours. It can have different aims: Diagnosis : obtaining a biopsy when it cannot be done another way. Cure : removing the whole tumour with a margin of healthy tissue and the nearby lymph nodes. Staging : finding out how far the cancer has really spread. Debulking : removing as much tumour as possible, as in ovarian cancer. Metastases : removing selected metastases, for example in the liver or lung in colorectal cancer. Palliation : relieving a blockage, bleeding or pain. Prevention :

d: About half of people with cancer receive radiotherapy at some point. How it works, the main types and the side effects it can cause.
n: How it works Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells, which find it harder to repair than normal cells do. It is aimed at a specific area of the body, so its effects are mostly limited to that area. About half of all cancer patients are estimated to need it at some point. What it is used for Radical : as the main curative treatment, for example in head and neck, cervical, prostate or inoperable lung cancer. Adjuvant : after surgery, to reduce the risk of local relapse , as after breast-conserving surgery. Neoadjuvant : before surgery, as in rectal cancer. Palliat

d: Cytotoxic drugs destroy fast-dividing cells. What they are used for, how they are given and how their side effects are prevented and treated.
n: What it is Chemotherapy is treatment with cytotoxic drugs, which damage cells that divide quickly, such as cancer cells. Because they also affect healthy fast-dividing cells (in the bone marrow, hair or gut), they cause characteristic side effects. It has been used since the 1940s, when nitrogen mustard was tested in lymphomas and aminopterin in childhood leukaemia . What it is used for To cure some cancers on its own, such as testicular cancer and many lymphomas and leukaemias. Neoadjuvant : before surgery, to shrink the tumour and test its sensitivity. d: Some cancers are driven by hormones. Blocking them is one of the most effective treatments for breast and prostate cancer.
n: What it is Some cancers use the body's hormones as fuel to grow: oestrogens in many breast and endometrial cancers, and androgens (such as testosterone) in prostate cancer. Hormone therapy (or endocrine therapy) reduces production of those hormones or blocks their action. It has nothing to do with menopause hormone treatment, and it is not chemotherapy . In breast cancer It is used for hormone receptor-positive tumours, about two in three: Tamoxifen : blocks the oestrogen receptor. Used before and after menopause. Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole, exemestane): reduce oestrogen prod

d: Drugs designed against a specific change in tumour cells. How they work, when they are used and why tumours often find a way round them.
n: What it is Targeted therapies act on a specific molecule the tumour needs to grow: a mutated protein, an excess protein or a signalling pathway. Unlike chemotherapy , which attacks any fast-dividing cell, they go after a specific weak spot in the cancer. They almost always require a biomarker showing the tumour has that target. The model was imatinib , approved in 2001 for chronic myeloid leukaemia : a daily tablet that blocks the BCR-ABL protein and controls the disease for years. Main types Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (names ending in "-tinib"): tablets that block enzymes that pass on growth

d: Treatments that help the immune system recognise and destroy cancer. How checkpoint inhibitors work, which cancers they are used in and what effects they can have.
n: The idea The immune system can recognise abnormal cells and destroy them, but tumours learn to hide or to put the brakes on lymphocytes. Immunotherapy tries to restore the immune system's ability to attack cancer. The idea is old: in the late 19th century the surgeon William Coley injected bacteria into patients with sarcoma , with inconsistent results. But modern immunotherapy began to change oncology from 2011. Checkpoint inhibitors T lymphocytes have natural "brakes", such as CTLA-4 and PD-1 , that stop them attacking healthy tissue. d: Blood stem cell transplants and CAR-T therapies are intensive treatments for some leukaemias, lymphomas and myelomas. What they are and how they work.
n: Blood stem cell transplant Often called a bone marrow transplant . It means giving blood stem cells (haematopoietic stem cells) to a person after intensive chemotherapy , sometimes with radiotherapy , that destroys their marrow. The new cells travel to the bones and start making blood again. There are two types: Autologous : the patient's own cells, collected before treatment. This allows very high doses of chemotherapy. d: Palliative care relieves pain and other symptoms and supports the person and their family. It is not only for the end of life: it can start at diagnosis.
n: What it is According to the WHO, palliative care improves the quality of life of people with serious illness and their families by preventing and relieving physical, psychological, social and spiritual suffering. It is provided by a team of doctors, nurses, psychologists and social workers, in hospital, in the community or at home. Not only for the end A common mistake is to think palliative care means "there is nothing more to be done". d: Simple, evidence-based recommendations anyone can follow to reduce their cancer risk. According to the WHO, between 30 and 50% of cancers could be prevented.
n: What it is The European Code Against Cancer is a set of recommendations drawn up by experts at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) with the support of the European Commission. It sums up what each person can do to reduce their risk, and what governments can do to make that easier. IARC updates it as new evidence emerges: check the current edition on its website. The main recommendations The recommendations of the fourth edition (2014), the most widely known, are: Do not smoke or use any form of tobacco. d: Avoidable cancer risk factors, ranked by how much they really matter. And why something being carcinogenic is not the same as how dangerous it is.
n: Tobacco comes first Tobacco is the leading avoidable cause of cancer . It causes most lung cancers and also cancers of the mouth, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, liver, kidney, bladder and cervix, and acute myeloid leukaemia . There is no safe level, and second-hand smoke also raises risk. Stopping smoking helps at any age : lung cancer risk falls steadily in the following years. Family doctors, stop-smoking services and medicines help people succeed. E-cigarettes are not harmless and are not recommended for non-smokers. d: Two routine vaccines, against hepatitis B and human papillomavirus, prevent cancer. How they work and who should have them.
n: Vaccines against infections that cause cancer There is no vaccine against "cancer" in general, but there are vaccines against two infections that cause a large share of infection-related cancers. Hepatitis B Hepatitis B virus can cause chronic liver infection that, over the years, leads to cirrhosis and liver cancer . The vaccine, available since the 1980s, was the first vaccine to prevent a cancer : in Taiwan, vaccinating newborns from 1984 clearly reduced liver cancer in vaccinated children and young people. d: Most of these symptoms are not caused by cancer, but if they last more than two or three weeks it is worth seeing a doctor. Earlier diagnosis improves the outlook.
n: A simple rule A symptom that is new , persistent (more than two or three weeks) or getting worse , with no clear explanation, deserves a visit to the doctor. It will almost always have a benign cause, but seeing someone in time allows cancer to be ruled out or diagnosed earlier. Do not wait for your next screening round. n: First: when to get help straight away During treatment, get help at once (following your team's instructions, or at an emergency department) if you have: A temperature of 38 °C or more, or shivering, especially during chemotherapy . Breathlessness , chest pain or a swollen leg. Severe or persistent diarrhoea , especially with immunotherapy . Vomiting that stops you drinking, bleeding, confusion or new weakness. d: What to eat during treatment, why "anti-cancer" diets do not work, and how exercise improves fatigue, quality of life and, in some cancers, the outlook.
n: During treatment The main goal is to maintain weight and muscle . Unintended weight loss makes treatment harder to tolerate. Some tips: Small, frequent meals , making the most of times when appetite is better. Enough protein : eggs, dairy, fish, meat, pulses. Good hydration . If your immunity is low, follow the food safety advice you are given (avoid risky raw foods, wash well, cook thoroughly). If you are losing weight or cannot eat, ask for a dietitian : there are supplements and strategies for every problem. Beware of myths No diet cures cancer. d: A cancer diagnosis affects the person and the whole family. Emotional reactions are normal, and asking for help is part of treatment.
n: Normal reactions to an abnormal situation Fear, sadness, anger, disbelief, guilt, anxiety about tests, trouble sleeping. These are expected reactions to a cancer diagnosis and do not mean something is wrong. They tend to come and go: there are better and worse days. About a third of people with cancer at some point have intense distress, anxiety or depression that needs specific attention. Ask for help if sadness or anxiety stops you functioning, lasts for weeks, you enjoy nothing, or you have thoughts that life is not worth living. d: Some treatments can affect fertility. Before starting, it is worth discussing the options to preserve it.
n: Why fertility is affected Chemotherapy , radiotherapy to the pelvis or brain, hormone therapy and some surgery can reduce or remove the ability to have children, temporarily or permanently. The risk depends on the treatment, dose and age. That is why guidelines recommend discussing fertility before treatment starts with everyone of reproductive age, and with the parents of children and teenagers. Preservation options For men Sperm banking , simple and effective, before treatment begins. For boys who do not yet produce sperm, freezing testicular tissue is experimental. d: Sick leave, returning to work, disability protection and the "right to be forgotten" for cancer survivors: what to know.
n: Time off work During treatment many people need sick leave . How long it lasts and how it is paid depend on each country's rules and the employment contract. Not everyone needs to be off the whole time: it depends on the job and the treatment. Returning to work Going back to work helps restore normality, but tiredness or brain fog can last months. Some options: Talk to occupational health to adapt the job or hours. Agree a phased return with your employer. Reduced hours, home working or a change of duties, where possible. d: More and more people live for many years after cancer. What follow-up they need, what late effects can appear and how to look after their health afterwards.
n: More and more survivors Thanks to earlier diagnosis and better treatment, survival has risen steadily. Worldwide there are more than 50 million people alive within five years of a cancer diagnosis, according to IARC estimates, and in the US alone more than 18 million cancer survivors. People are usually called long-term survivors five years after diagnosis without disease, though each cancer has its own timescales. d: The London surgeon who in 1775 described chimney sweeps' cancer and showed, for the first time, that a cancer could have an avoidable environmental cause.
n: An observant surgeon Percivall Pott was one of the most respected surgeons of 18th-century London, at St Bartholomew's Hospital. His name survives in several conditions, such as tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease) and a type of ankle fracture. The chimney sweeps In 1775 he published brief observations on cancer of the scrotum in chimney sweeps . They were boys who started work at four or five, often naked, climbing narrow chimneys. Soot stayed in the folds of their skin for years. Pott saw that many of them developed, while still young, a cancer that was extremely rare in other people,

d: The Polish physicist and chemist who discovered polonium and radium, won two Nobel Prizes and drove the use of radioactivity to treat cancer.
n: From Warsaw to Paris Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, then under Russian rule, where women could not attend university. She studied in secret and in 1891 moved to Paris, where she took degrees in physics and mathematics. There she met Pierre Curie, whom she married in 1895. Radioactivity Inspired by Henri Becquerel's discovery that uranium gave off rays, Marie studied the phenomenon, which she named radioactivity . In 1898, with Pierre, she discovered two new elements: polonium , named after her country, and radium . In 1903 they shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Becquerel; Marie was

d: The Greek doctor who invented the smear test that bears his name, the first mass cancer screening test, which has prevented millions of deaths from cervical cancer.
n: An immigrant in New York Georgios Papanikolaou trained as a doctor in Athens and as a zoologist in Germany. In 1913 he emigrated to the United States with his wife, Andromache Mavroyeni (Mary), with no money and no English. He worked as a carpet salesman and a restaurant violinist before getting a post at Cornell University in New York. From guinea pigs to cancer Studying changes in vaginal cells of guinea pigs through the cycle, and later of women, including Mary, who had daily smears for years, he noticed in 1928 that some samples contained cancer cells . He presented it at a conference unde

d: The Boston pathologist who in 1948 achieved the first drug-induced remissions of childhood leukaemia and is considered the father of modern chemotherapy.
n: A pathologist among children Sidney Farber was a pathologist at Boston Children's Hospital. In the 1940s, acute childhood leukaemia was a death sentence: children died within weeks, with no possible treatment. Aminopterin Folic acid was known to be needed to make blood cells. Farber first tried giving folate to children with leukaemia, and the disease got worse. So he thought of the opposite: blocking folate. With antifolate drugs synthesised by Yellapragada SubbaRow and the Lederle company, such as aminopterin , he treated 16 children. In 1948 he reported that 10 had temporary remissions . Th

d: The British nurse, social worker and doctor who founded the modern palliative care movement and the concept of "total pain".
n: Three professions Cicely Saunders was first a nurse , during the Second World War, until a back injury took her out of the profession. She then trained as a medical social worker . Seeing how dying patients were treated in hospitals, she realised she needed a doctor's authority to change things and, at 33, studied medicine . Total pain She researched the regular use of morphine, given on a schedule to prevent pain rather than waiting for it to appear. And she proposed the concept of "total pain" : the suffering of a person with advanced illness has a physical dimension, but also psychological,

d: The surgeon who in 1971 proposed that tumours must grow blood vessels in order to grow, an idea that opened the way to anti-angiogenic drugs.
n: An observation in the Navy While working for the US Navy in the 1960s, Judah Folkman grew tumours in isolated organs. He noticed that tumours stopped growing once they reached a few millimetres, and that they did not form blood vessels in those organs. Starving the tumour In 1971 he published his hypothesis in The New England Journal of Medicine : tumours need to form new blood vessels ( angiogenesis ) to grow beyond a small size, and blocking that process could be a treatment. The idea was met with scepticism for years; many thought the vessels were simply an inflammatory reaction. From hypot

d: The surgeon whose rigorous clinical trials showed that breast cancer did not need mutilating surgery to be cured, and changed how the disease is understood.
n: Against radical mastectomy For almost a century breast cancer was treated with the Halsted radical mastectomy , which removed the breast, chest muscles and armpit lymph nodes. It was based on the idea that cancer spread in an orderly way and that the more removed, the better. Bernard Fisher, a surgeon at the University of Pittsburgh, proposed another hypothesis: breast cancer may be a systemic disease from the start, with cells travelling in the blood, and the extent of local surgery does not by itself determine survival. The NSABP trials Leading the NSABP cooperative group, he organised large

d: The Madrid biochemist whose team identified in 1982 the mutation that activates the first human oncogene, RAS, and who led Spain's National Cancer Research Centre.
n: The first human oncogene Mariano Barbacid earned his PhD in chemistry at the Complutense University of Madrid and in 1974 moved to the US National Cancer Institute. There his group searched for genes able to turn normal cells into cancer cells. In 1982, almost at the same time as the groups of Robert Weinberg and Michael Wigler, his team isolated an oncogene from a human bladder tumour: an altered version of the HRAS gene. That same year they identified the cause of its activation: a point mutation , a change in a single letter of DNA, which altered one amino acid of the protein. It was the fi

d: The oncologist who brought imatinib to patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia and turned a fatal disease into a chronic condition controlled with a tablet.
n: A perfect target Chronic myeloid leukaemia has a single, known cause: the Philadelphia chromosome , discovered in 1960, which creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene. Its protein is a tyrosine kinase that is always switched on, telling cells to multiply. In the 1990s chemists at Ciba-Geigy (later Novartis), including Nicholas Lydon, designed molecules able to block kinases. Brian Druker, an oncologist in Portland, Oregon, showed in the laboratory that one of them, STI571, killed leukaemia cells without harming normal ones, and pushed to get it to patients. The trial In the first trial, published in 20

d: The two immunologists who discovered how to release the immune system's brakes to attack cancer, and won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
n: The immune system's brakes T lymphocytes carry molecules that act as brakes to stop them attacking healthy tissue. Two researchers, working separately, studied two of them. James Allison and CTLA-4 James Allison, at the University of California, Berkeley, studied the protein CTLA-4 . He reasoned that blocking it might let lymphocytes attack tumours. In 1996 he showed that an antibody against CTLA-4 made tumours disappear in mice. It took years to convince industry. The resulting drug, ipilimumab , was approved in 2011 for advanced melanoma, and some treated patients are still alive more than t

d: What a clinical trial is, what its phases mean, how to find out if there is one for you and what to ask before taking part.
n: What it is A clinical trial is a study in people that tests whether a new treatment (or a new way of using a known one) is safe and effective , usually by comparing it with standard treatment. Every cancer drug used today went through clinical trials first, with thousands of patients taking part. The phases Phase Main question Participants I Is it safe? What dose? Tens, often with different tumours II Does it work against this cancer? Tens or hundreds III Is it better than standard treatment? Hundreds or thousands, randomly assigned IV What happens in real practice, long term? Patients treated

d: Choosing treatment according to the molecular features of each tumour. What already works, its limits and why it does not mean tailor-made treatment for everyone.
n: The idea For decades cancer was treated according to the organ where it started. Precision medicine adds another question: which molecular changes drive this particular tumour? If one of them is a treatable target, a drug aimed at it can be chosen. What already works In advanced non-small cell lung cancer , patients with changes in EGFR , ALK , ROS1 and other genes take targeted tablets that have multiplied their survival. In breast cancer , HER2 and hormone receptors have guided treatment for decades. In chronic myeloid leukaemia and GIST , imatinib. In melanoma , BRAF and MEK inhibitors. Tum

d: Antibody-drug conjugates, bispecifics, mRNA vaccines, KRAS inhibitors and cell therapies: what the new treatments in the news are and where they stand.
n: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) An antibody-drug conjugate is an antibody carrying a very potent chemotherapy payload attached by a chemical linker. It recognises a protein on tumour cells, enters them and releases the drug inside. They are called "Trojan horses". Trastuzumab deruxtecan has changed treatment for breast cancers with low HER2 levels, and enfortumab vedotin for bladder cancer. They have their own side effects, such as eye or lung problems depending on the product. Bispecific antibodies They recognise two targets at once: one on the tumour cell and one on the T lymphocyte, which t

d: "New drug cures cancer", "this food prevents tumours". Ten questions to tell real advances from empty promises.
n: Why it matters Every week there are headlines about "the cure for cancer". Behind them may be an important advance, a preliminary result in mice or a marketing campaign. For someone living with cancer, false hope or a false alarm has a real cost. Ten questions Who was it tested in? Cells, mice or people. Many treatments that work in the lab fail in humans. How many people? Ten patients are not the same as ten thousand. What was it compared with? A treatment with no comparison group can look effective for reasons unrelated to it. What phase of study? d: A simple explanation: what happens in cells, why it is not a single disease and how it spreads.
n: Cells that lose control The body is made of trillions of cells that divide, do their job and die in an orderly way, following the instructions in their genes. Cancer appears when a cell builds up changes in its DNA that make it divide out of control, ignore signals to stop or die, and escape the body's defences. These changes mainly affect two kinds of genes: oncogenes , which act like a stuck accelerator, and tumour suppressor genes , brakes that stop working. They usually build up over years, through chance errors in DNA copying, age and exposures such as tobacco or ultraviolet light. That i

d: All cancers are genetic, but very few are inherited. When to think about a family predisposition.
n: Genetic is not the same as inherited Cancer is always a genetic disease, because it arises from changes in cells' DNA. But almost all those changes are acquired during life in a particular cell, and are not passed on to children. Only 5 to 10% of cancers are due to an inherited variant that greatly increases risk, such as those in BRCA1 and BRCA2 or in Lynch syndrome . Having a relative with cancer Cancer is common: about one in two or three people will have it during their lifetime. So it is normal for almost every family to have cases, without that meaning an inherited predisposition. Someti

d: A figure seen everywhere that often frightens people. What it measures, what it doesn't, and why it is nobody's deadline.
n: What it measures Five-year survival is the percentage of people in a group still alive five years after diagnosis. If it is 80% for a cancer, it means that of every hundred people diagnosed in a given period, about eighty were still alive five years later. Registries often use net survival , which removes deaths from other causes, so countries and periods can be compared. What it does not mean It is not a deadline : it does not mean people live only five years. Many live for decades, and for many cancers reaching five years without disease is practically a cure. It does not predict what will h

t: What do remission and cure mean?
d: Complete remission, partial remission, stable disease, cure: the words used to describe response to treatment.
n: Response to treatment Complete remission (or complete response): tests find no signs of cancer. Very good news, although disease may remain in undetectable amounts. Partial remission (or partial response): the cancer has shrunk substantially, for example by more than 30% in the size of measurable tumours. Stable disease : it is neither growing nor shrinking significantly. In advanced disease, keeping cancer stable with good quality of life is a worthwhile goal. Progression : the cancer grows or new lesions appear. Minimal residual disease In leukaemias, lymphomas and myelomas, very sensitive t

t: Do biopsies or surgery spread cancer?
d: A common fear that delays diagnosis. What studies say about biopsies, surgery and "air" reaching the tumour.
n: The short answer Not in normal practice. The risk of a needle biopsy spreading tumour cells along its track is very low , and doctors take steps to reduce it further, such as planning the needle's path. Delaying or avoiding a biopsy out of fear is dangerous, because without it the type of cancer cannot be known or the right treatment chosen. Studies of thousands of patients, for example in breast or prostate cancer, have not shown that biopsy worsens survival. Special cases In some tumours the biopsy should be done, or at least planned, by the team that will operate, as with sarcomas , so the

t: Myths about the causes of cancer
d: Sugar, mobile phones, deodorants, stress, sweeteners or microwaves. What the evidence says about the most repeated worries.
n: "Sugar feeds cancer" All cells, healthy ones too, use glucose. Eating sugar does not specifically make a tumour grow, and cutting it out completely does not cure it. What does matter is that excess calories lead to obesity , which increases the risk of several cancers. "Mobile phones cause brain cancer" IARC classified them in 2011 as "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B) on limited evidence. Later studies, including a review commissioned by the WHO in 2024, have found no increase in brain tumour risk, despite the huge rise in use. "Deodorants and bras cause breast cancer" There is no evidence th

d: The difference between complementary therapies, which can help people feel better, and alternative therapies, which replace treatment and put lives at risk.
n: Complementary is not the same as alternative A complementary therapy is used alongside medical treatment to ease symptoms or improve wellbeing: exercise, yoga, meditation, massage, acupuncture for some nausea, or music therapy. Some have evidence of benefit for quality of life, and hospitals include them in what is called integrative oncology . An alternative therapy is used instead of medical treatment, with the promise of curing cancer. None has proven it. t: Why is there more cancer than before?
d: The number of cases is rising, but the risk of dying from cancer at each age is falling. The reasons are ageing, earlier diagnosis and some habits.
n: More cases, lower death rates by age It is true that more cancers are diagnosed each year: worldwide, cases rose from about 14 million in 2012 to about 20 million in 2022. But that does not mean cancer is "a modern epidemic". There are several explanations: Ageing : cancer is much more common with age, and we are living longer. This is the main reason. Population growth . Better diagnosis : screening and imaging find more tumours, sometimes ones that would never have caused problems. Changing habits : smoking among women from the 1970s, obesity, inactivity and alcohol. When people of the same

t: Can I ask for a second opinion?
d: Yes. Asking another specialist to review the diagnosis or treatment plan is a patient's right. When it can help and how to do it.
n: A right, not a sign of distrust Most health systems recognise patients' right to information, to decide about their own treatment and to seek a second opinion , especially for serious illnesses such as cancer. Good professionals understand this and provide reports and test results. When it can help A rare cancer or a difficult diagnosis, such as some sarcomas or lymphomas. When very different treatment options are being considered, or very complex surgery. If the situation has not been explained well or you are unsure about the decision. t: How can I support someone with cancer?
d: What to say and what not to, how to offer useful help and how to look after yourself when a relative or friend has cancer.
n: Being there matters more than getting it right There are no perfect words. What many people with cancer value most is that others don't disappear . A message, a short visit or a call is worth more than silence for fear of saying the wrong thing. What tends to help Listening without rushing and letting the person decide what to talk about, including things other than cancer. Asking "how are you today?" rather than "how are you?". Offering specific help : "I'll drive you to hospital on Tuesday", "I'll bring dinner on Thursday", "I'll have the children on Saturday". Respecting their decisions abo

d: Treatment given after the main treatment, usually surgery, to reduce the risk of relapse. It may be chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormone therapy or immunotherapy.
The formation of new blood vessels. Tumours stimulate it to get oxygen and nutrients, and some drugs block it.
An antibody linked to a very potent drug, which it delivers directly to cells carrying its target. Also called an ADC.
A tumour that does not invade nearby tissue or spread. It can cause problems through its size or location, but it is not a cancer.
A measurable feature that tells us about a tumour: for example a hormone receptor, HER2, a mutation or PD-L1. It helps choose treatment.
Taking a tissue sample to examine under the microscope. It is the test that confirms the diagnosis of most cancers.
Radiotherapy in which the radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumour. Used, for example, in cervical or prostate cancer.
Genes that help repair DNA. Inherited variants that inactivate them greatly increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer.
A treatment in which a patient's T cells are collected, modified in the laboratory to recognise cancer cells and infused back.
An agent that can cause cancer, such as tobacco smoke, asbestos or ultraviolet radiation. IARC classifies them by the strength of the evidence.
Cancer arising from epithelial cells, which line the skin, organs and glands. It is the most common type of cancer.
A lesion with malignant cells that have not yet broken through the layer where they started. It does not spread, but may progress if untreated.
A drug that blocks the immune system's "brakes", such as PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4, so that lymphocytes attack the tumour.
Treatment with drugs that destroy fast-dividing cells. It can cure, reduce the risk of relapse or control the disease.
A study in people comparing a new treatment with the usual treatment to find out whether it is effective and safe. It has phases and eligibility criteria.
The percentage of people in a group still alive five years after diagnosis. It is a statistical measure, not a deadline.
Describes a genetic variant present in every cell of the body from birth. It can be inherited. The opposite of somatic.
A description of how different tumour cells look from normal cells under the microscope. A high grade usually means faster growth.
A protein that, when present in excess in breast or stomach tumour cells, drives their growth. There are specific drugs against it.
Treatment that blocks or reduces the hormones that drive some cancers, mainly breast and prostate cancer.
Human papillomavirus. Some types cause almost all cervical cancers and some anal, penile, vulvar and oropharyngeal cancers. There is a vaccine.
A laboratory technique that stains specific proteins in a tissue sample. It helps identify a tumour's type and which treatments may work.
Treatment that helps the immune system recognise and destroy cancer cells.
Cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. It can be acute or chronic, and lymphoid or myeloid.
A test of blood or other fluids looking for fragments of tumour DNA or other signs of cancer. It has specific uses, and others still under research.
Cancer of lymphocytes that usually affects the lymph nodes. Divided into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
An inherited predisposition to colorectal, endometrial and other cancers, caused by variants in DNA repair genes.
A tumour able to invade nearby tissue and spread to other organs. A synonym for cancer.
The time at which half the people in a study are still alive. The other half live longer. It does not predict what will happen to one person.
A tumour formed by cells that have broken away from the original tumour and travelled to another organ in the blood or lymph.
A sign that the tumour cell does not correct DNA copying errors properly. Linked to Lynch syndrome and predicts a good response to immunotherapy.
A laboratory-made protein that recognises a specific target, for example a protein on the surface of tumour cells. Names end in "-mab".
Cancer of the plasma cells in the bone marrow, which make antibodies. It can affect the bones, kidneys and blood.
Treatment given before the main treatment, usually surgery, to shrink the tumour and see how it responds.
Abnormal, uncontrolled growth of cells. It can be benign or malignant. "Malignant neoplasm" means cancer.
Survival attributable to cancer, removing deaths from other causes. It is used to compare countries and periods.
A fall in neutrophils, white blood cells that fight infection. A common effect of chemotherapy. Fever with neutropenia is an emergency.
A gene that, when altered, pushes the cell to divide out of control. It works like a stuck accelerator.
The medical specialty that deals with cancer. It includes medical, radiation, surgical and paediatric oncology and haemato-oncology.
Care that relieves symptoms and suffering and supports the family at any stage of a serious illness. It is not limited to the last days.
The medical specialty that studies tissues and cells under the microscope. The pathologist's report confirms whether there is cancer and what type.
A protein some tumour cells use to put the brakes on lymphocytes. Measuring it helps decide on some immunotherapies.
The expected course of a disease. In cancer it depends on the type, stage, tumour biology, the person and the response to treatment.
Treatment that uses ionising radiation to destroy cancer cells in a specific area of the body.
The return of a cancer after a period in which it could not be detected. Also called recurrence.
A decrease in or disappearance of signs of cancer. Complete remission means no disease is detected with available tests.
Cancer arising in bone or soft tissues, such as muscle, fat or blood vessels. It is uncommon.
A programme offering a test to people without symptoms to find a cancer or precancerous change in time. Breast, bowel and cervical screening are the most common.
A review of the diagnosis or treatment by another specialist or centre. It is a patient's right and should not offend the team.
Describes a genetic change that appears in a cell during life, for example in a tumour. It is not inherited.
A description of how far a cancer has spread: its size, whether it affects lymph nodes and whether it has reached other organs. Usually given from 0 to IV.
An infusion of blood stem cells, the patient's own or from a donor, after intensive chemotherapy. Often called a bone marrow transplant.
A drug that acts on a specific change in tumour cells, such as a mutation or an excess protein. It usually requires a biomarker.
A system for describing the stage of many solid tumours: T is the size or extent of the tumour, N the lymph nodes affected and M metastases.
A mass of abnormal tissue. It can be benign or malignant. Not all tumours are cancers.
A substance measured in the blood that can be raised in some cancers, such as PSA or CEA. It almost never diagnoses cancer on its own.
A gene that slows cell division or repairs damage. When it is lost, the cell loses a brake. Examples: TP53, RB1, BRCA1.
